subject: PPC for an ordered logistic model

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: PPC for an ordered logistic model
parts:
Hi Staners,

A colleague brought me an interesting data set consisting of a somewhat elaborate experimental design investigating sharing behaviour by children. There are multiple experimental manipulations, and in each we observe the number of stickers (0-10) shared by a child. I coded this up as an ordered logistic regression model (akin to section 8.8 of version 2.13.1 of the manual, but it was a hierarchical design so I had to add that bit in as well), but I'm a little concerned whether this is an appropriate model because a quick look at the histogram of the number of stickers shared seems to have a large number of 0s, inducing some seeming bimodality. So I coded up a posterior predictive check:



Red points-and-lines are the observed counts in the data, bars are the posterior 50% intervals. Since the interval for the 0s does indeed cover the data, I might reasonably put aside my concern, correct?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] PPC for an ordered logistic model
parts:
I recommend removing the horizontal bars on your graph as they draw attention to the endpoints of the intervals, and those endpoints don't convey any particularly relevant information.
A

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] PPC for an ordered logistic model
parts:
On one hand the center of the posterior seems to be overfititng to the data,
but on the other hand the breadth of the posterior remains sufficiently wide
so that the entire posterior isn’t overfitting much.  You might want to try
splitting the data in two, fitting on one half and using the other half for the
PPC to see if it’s any different.

There might be more sophisticated correlations between the categories
that you’re not modeling which pulls the measurement variation to larger
values to compensate.  You could also try an explicitly zero-infated model
to see if that allow the model to better capture the lower categories.
